_note: The atlas glossary. Copy strings mark a term as [[id|text]]; pages show the short definition on hover and link here. Plain words, no em dashes.

terms.short: OpenAI’s grouping of related papers around one headline result. The release has 372, numbered 001 to 377 with five numbers unused.
The main claim OpenAI’s catalogue gives for a family. A family’s Lean statements may state all of it, part of it, or a supporting step.

A Lean file that states one theorem and leaves its proof open, with a configuration naming the theorem, the definitions a solution may supply and the axioms it may use. The release has 416. The atlas calls each one a Lean statement.
The Lean tool that checks a solution against a Lean statement. If it accepts, the solution proves the configured theorem using only the allowed axioms, and the Lean kernel accepts every step.
Lean’s placeholder for a missing proof. A Lean statement leaves its proof as sorry on purpose; the proof is in OpenAI’s separate solution module.
The axioms a configuration allows a proof to use, here the three standard ones: propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. A replay shows which ones a proof actually uses.
A definition a configuration lists for the solution to supply. Comparator compares it by name and type only, so its body comes from the solution and must be read there.
The small core of Lean that checks every step of a proof. Everything Lean accepts passes through it.
An independent type checker for Lean written in Rust. Comparator can run it beside Lean’s own kernel as a second check; OpenAI’s configurations switch it on for 2 of the 416 Lean statements.
Lean’s community library of formalised mathematics. OpenAI’s library pins its own version of it.
OpenAI’s note on what a family’s Lean statements cover, in lean/docs of the release. The atlas quotes it beside other people’s readings.
A run of Comparator on OpenAI’s solution by a group outside OpenAI, at the release’s pinned commit. The atlas shows each group’s verdict, credited and dated.

MathVet and Carlos Toledo’s cert-machine, who each read every family’s Lean statements against its headline, independently of OpenAI and of each other, under their own published rules. Each states its own method; the atlas quotes their verdicts and notes and adds none of its own.
A proof assistant independent of Lean. Ben Knill’s cards check selected steps of eleven families in it, with negative controls that must fail.
A computation that decides a finite claim in a paper exactly, written independently from the paper. Certified means the published object has the claimed property; undecided is no evidence against it.
A link between a paper’s statement and a Lean statement, chosen automatically by the words they share. Nobody has reviewed it; it shows where to read, never that the two say the same thing.
The atlas’s HTML version of a paper, converted from its TeX at the pinned commit. The PDF stays the reference; a page that did not convert in full lists what is missing.
A paper OpenAI removed after the release, with a notice explaining the gap. The atlas keeps it, marked, under the family it was listed in on release day.
A paper OpenAI later replaced with a revised edition. The atlas keeps the earlier edition, marked, beside the current one in the same family.

One of the two outside readers. It reads each family’s Lean statements against the headline under a published rubric, with help from a model, and runs Comparator itself. Its verdict and note are quoted in its own terms.

Carlos Toledo’s audit of the release, one of the two outside readers. It re-runs every Lean statement through Comparator with nanoda switched on, reads each family’s Lean statements against the headline clause by clause, and decides finite parts of some papers with exact code.
The definitions a Lean statement makes for itself before stating its theorem, found by reading its text. Each is a meaning a reader must check against the paper, because Mathlib does not supply it.

terms.term: Paired from the Lean statement’s own words
terms.short: The atlas chose the paper statement whose words best match the Lean statement’s own text, and only when one statement was a clear match. Nobody has reviewed it.

terms.term: Paired from the catalogue’s words, as a fallback
terms.short: When the Lean text matched no paper statement clearly, the atlas used the candidate chosen from the words of OpenAI’s catalogue, and only when that candidate is in the Lean statement’s own paper. Nobody has reviewed it.

terms.term: A Lean statement with no confident match
terms.short: Neither the Lean text nor the catalogue words picked out one paper statement clearly, so the atlas pairs nothing and lists the closest statements instead.

terms.term: Paired by a citation in the Lean source
terms.short: The Lean source cites the paper statement it formalises, and the atlas records that link as written. Nobody has checked that the two say the same thing.

terms.term: Paired by the release’s own declaration
terms.short: The release’s own manifest binds the Lean statement to a paper statement, and the atlas records that binding as written. Nobody has checked that the two say the same thing.
